props.title: Wild Side
props.initialSlug: Cop goes undercover to catch vicious serial killer

sections.content: **Wild Side** (1995) represents a fascinating entry in 1990s neo-noir, starring Christopher Walken and Anne Heche in a twisted tale of manipulation and sexuality. The film follows similar thematic territory as Basic Instinct (1992) and **Body of Evidence** (1993), exploring dangerous liaisons and power dynamics through a noir lens. Director Donald Cammell, who previously directed the cult classic **Performance** (1970), brings his signature psychosexual style to this underappreciated thriller, though the film suffered from studio interference and multiple cuts.

sections.content: Like many neo-noirs of the 1990s, **Wild Side** (1995) plays with traditional genre expectations while incorporating more explicit content and sexual themes. The film shares DNA with **Bound** (1996) and **Red Rock West** (1993) in its exploration of criminal schemes and double-crosses. Christopher Walken delivers one of his most menacing performances as Bruno, continuing the trend of memorable noir villains he portrayed in films like **King of New York** (1990).

The troubled production history of **Wild Side** (1995) mirrors other complex studio battles of the era, similar to what happened with **Once Upon a Time in America** (1984) and **Heaven's Gate** (1980). Director Donald Cammell fought for his original vision but ultimately lost control of the final cut, leading to his suicide in 1996. The film exists in multiple versions, with the director's cut offering a more cohesive and artistically daring vision than the theatrical release. SUBHEAD: Sexual Politics and Power Dynamics

sections.content: The film's treatment of sexuality and power relationships reflects the changing landscape of 1990s thrillers, following in the wake of **Fatal Attraction** (1987) and **Sea of Love** (1989). Anne Heche's complex performance as Alex navigates similar territory to Linda Fiorentino's work in The Last Seduction (1994), challenging traditional gender roles within the noir framework. The film's exploration of bisexuality was notably progressive for its time, predating similar themes in later works like **Mulholland Drive** (2001).
